'''Allison Jane Doupe''' (1954 – 24 October 2014) was a Canadian psychiatrist, biologist, and neuroscientist. She is best known for her pioneering work in [[bird|avian]] [[neurobiology]] that linked birdsong to human language, showing that birds and humans learn to communicate in similar ways.<ref>{{cite journal |last1 = Insel |first1 = TR |last2 = Landis |first2 = S |title = Allison Doupe (1954-2014) |journal = Nature |year = 2014 |volume = 515 |issue = 7527 |page = 344 |doi = 10.1038/515344a |pmid=25409820|bibcode = 2014Natur.515..344I |doi-access = free }}</ref> In 2014, Doupe was awarded the [[Pradel Research Award]] by the [[National Academy of Sciences]] for her work on [[Neural circuit|neural circuits]] and information processing in [[songbirds]], which she pioneered as a model species for studying learning and memory.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nasonline.org/about-nas/awards/pradel-research-award.html |title=Pradel Research Award |publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]] |access-date=March 11, 2017 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150102150453/http://www.nasonline.org/about-nas/awards/pradel-research-award.html |archive-date=January 2, 2015 }}</ref>

==Life==
After graduating from [[McGill University]], Doupe obtained her MD and PhD in Neurobiology from [[Harvard University]]. She joined the [[University of California, San Francisco]] Departments of Psychiatry and Physiology in 1993 as an assistant professor, and was promoted to full professor in 2000.<ref name="InMemoriam">{{cite web| url = https://psych.ucsf.edu/doupe/| title = In Memoriam: Allison Doupe, MD, PhD| date = October 27, 2014 | publisher = University of California, San Francisco Department of Psychiatry | access-date = January 2, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Barondes|first1=Samuel|last2=Stryker|first2=Michael P.|date=February 2015|title=Allison Doupe: In Memoriam|journal=Neuron|volume=85|issue=4|pages=667–668|doi=10.1016/j.neuron.2015.01.030|pmid=25848665|issn=0896-6273|doi-access=free}}</ref>  

In 2008 she was elected as a fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ucsf.edu/news/2008/04/8061/four-elected-american-academy-arts-sciences|title=Four Elected to American Academy of Arts & Sciences|website=UC San Francisco|date=30 April 2008 |language=en|access-date=2018-10-09}}</ref>

She died on 24 October 2014, of cancer.<ref name="InMemoriam" />
